sections.skill: Read a pay stub and calculate deductions and net pay

questions.prompt: Which amount on a pay stub is the money actually deposited into the worker's bank account?

choices.text: Net pay
Gross pay
Year-to-date gross
Total deductions

questions.intro: A pay stub (pay statement) shows: gross pay; deductions, which are amounts taken out for taxes, retirement, insurance, and more; net pay, which is gross pay minus deductions; and year-to-date (YTD) totals. Net pay is your take-home pay.
questions.feedback: Net pay = gross pay − deductions, and it is the amount deposited.

misconceptions.C: Confuses this period with the year total
misconceptions.D: Confuses money taken out with money received

sources: IRS (Topic 751): Employee Social Security tax is 6.2% (up to the annual wage base) and Medicare tax is 1.45% of wages. (https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751)

questions.prompt: Gabriel's gross pay is $1,200.00. The Social Security tax rate for employees is 6.2%. How much Social Security tax is withheld?
questions.intro: FICA taxes fund Social Security and Medicare. Employees pay 6.2% of wages for Social Security (up to a yearly wage limit) and 1.45% for Medicare. The employer pays a matching amount.
sources: IRS (Topic 751): Employee Social Security tax is 6.2% (up to the annual wage base) and Medicare tax is 1.45% of wages. (https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751)

questions.prompt:
Pay stub (biweekly): Gross pay $1,200.00 | 401(k) contribution (pre-tax) $60.00 | Federal income tax $88.00 | Social Security $74.40 | Medicare $17.40 | State income tax $22.80
What is Gabriel's net pay?
questions.intro: To find net pay, add all the deductions, then subtract the total from gross pay. Retirement contributions are deductions too, even though the money is still yours in a retirement account.

misconceptions.A: Gives total deductions instead of net pay

sources: IRS (Topic 751): Employee Social Security tax is 6.2% (up to the annual wage base) and Medicare tax is 1.45% of wages. (https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751)

questions.prompt:
Pay stub (biweekly): Gross pay $1,200.00 | 401(k) contribution (pre-tax) $60.00 | Federal income tax $88.00 | Social Security $74.40 | Medicare $17.40 | State income tax $22.80
Which deduction is money Gabriel still owns after it leaves his paycheck?

choices.text: The federal income tax
The Social Security tax
The state income tax
The 401(k) contribution

questions.intro: Deductions go to different places. Income taxes and Social Security and Medicare taxes are sent to the government. Retirement plan contributions are deposited into an account in the worker's name.
questions.feedback: A 401(k) contribution goes into his own retirement account. Taxes withheld are paid to the government (any overpaid income tax comes back as a refund).

misconceptions.A: Thinks withheld tax is still his
misconceptions.C: Thinks withheld tax is still his

sections.relationship: Students who confuse gross and net pay cannot read a pay stub or budget correctly.

questions.prompt: Ivy's job offer says "$18 per hour." Her first paycheck is smaller than 18 × her hours. Why?

choices.text: Deductions were taken from her gross pay
Her employer made an error by paying less than promised
The bank charged a fee for depositing her paycheck
Her hourly wage was lowered in her first week

questions.correct_answer: Deductions were taken from her gross pay
questions.intro: Many workers have their paychecks deposited into bank accounts. The amount deposited is net pay: gross pay minus deductions such as taxes and benefit costs. Gross pay is what you earned; net pay is what you receive.
questions.feedback: Deductions explain the difference between gross pay (18 × hours) and net pay.

misconceptions.B: Expects net pay to equal gross pay

sources: IRS (Topic 751): Employee Social Security tax is 6.2% (up to the annual wage base) and Medicare tax is 1.45% of wages. (https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751)

questions.intro: Net pay = gross pay − total deductions.

questions.prompt:
Pay stub (biweekly): Gross pay $1,200.00 | 401(k) contribution (pre-tax) $60.00 | Federal income tax $88.00 | Social Security $74.40 | Medicare $17.40 | State income tax $22.80
The 401(k) contribution is pre-tax for federal income tax. What are Gabriel's federal taxable wages for this paycheck?
questions.intro: A pre-tax deduction is taken out before income tax is figured, which lowers taxable wages. A traditional 401(k) contribution is pre-tax for income tax, but Social Security and Medicare taxes still apply to it.
sources: IRS (Topic 751): Employee Social Security tax is 6.2% (up to the annual wage base) and Medicare tax is 1.45% of wages. (https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751)

questions.prompt:
Pay stub (biweekly): Gross pay $1,200.00 | 401(k) contribution (pre-tax) $60.00 | Federal income tax $88.00 | Social Security $74.40 | Medicare $17.40 | State income tax $22.80
Why are Social Security and Medicare figured on $1,200.00, not on $1,140.00 (gross pay minus the pre-tax 401(k) contribution)?

choices.text: 401(k) deferrals are still subject to FICA
The payroll system made an error
FICA taxes are figured on net pay
Social Security is optional for young workers

questions.correct_answer: 401(k) deferrals are still subject to FICA
questions.feedback: 401(k) deferrals reduce income-taxable wages but not the wages used for Social Security and Medicare.

misconceptions.C: Confuses the FICA base with net pay

questions.prompt: Gabriel's federal tax rate on his last dollars of income is 12%. If he contributes $60 pre-tax, about how much does his take-home pay drop?
questions.intro: Because pre-tax contributions lower taxable income, they also lower income tax. Contributing $60 pre-tax reduces take-home pay by less than $60.
questions.feedback: Tax saved: $60 × 0.12 = $7.20. Take-home drops by $60 − $7.20 = $52.80 (before any state tax effect).
sources: IRS (Topic 751): Employee Social Security tax is 6.2% (up to the annual wage base) and Medicare tax is 1.45% of wages. (https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751)

questions.prompt: A Roth 401(k) contribution is an after-tax deduction. Compared with a traditional (pre-tax) 401(k) contribution of the same amount today, it…

choices.text: lowers today's take-home pay more, but qualified withdrawals later are tax-free
lowers today's take-home pay less and is taxed again later
has no effect on take-home pay
is not allowed for workers under 25

questions.correct_answer: lowers today's take-home pay more, but qualified withdrawals later are tax-free
questions.intro: After-tax deductions are taken out after income tax is figured. Roth retirement contributions are after-tax: no tax break now, but qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.
questions.feedback: Roth contributions do not reduce taxable income now, so take-home falls by the full amount; qualified withdrawals later are tax-free.
sources: IRS (Topic 751): Employee Social Security tax is 6.2% (up to the annual wage base) and Medicare tax is 1.45% of wages. (https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751)

questions.prompt: Which deduction is usually AFTER-tax?

choices.text: A traditional 401(k) contribution
A health insurance premium through a cafeteria plan
A health savings account (HSA) payroll contribution
Union dues taken from pay

questions.feedback: Union dues are typically after-tax. Traditional 401(k), cafeteria-plan health premiums, and HSA payroll contributions are typically pre-tax.

sections.skill: Year-to-date totals and checking for errors

questions.prompt: Gabriel has received 10 biweekly paychecks of $1,200.00 gross this year. What should his YTD gross pay show?
questions.intro: Year-to-date (YTD) amounts add up everything since January 1. They help you check totals and match your Form W-2 at year end.
sources: IRS (Topic 751): Employee Social Security tax is 6.2% (up to the annual wage base) and Medicare tax is 1.45% of wages. (https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751)

questions.prompt: Gabriel worked 84 hours in a two-week period, including 4 overtime hours in the second week, but his stub shows 84 regular hours and no overtime. What should he do?

choices.text: Ask payroll to correct it, bringing his own record of hours
Ignore it; pay stubs cannot contain mistakes
Wait for his tax refund to fix it
Work fewer hours next week to even it out

questions.correct_answer: Ask payroll to correct it, bringing his own record of hours
questions.feedback: Keeping your own record of hours lets you spot and correct payroll mistakes such as missing overtime.

misconceptions.D: Does not fix the missing pay

sources: IRS (Topic 751): Employee Social Security tax is 6.2% (up to the annual wage base) and Medicare tax is 1.45% of wages. (https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751)

questions.prompt: Gabriel's YTD Social Security is $744.00 on YTD gross of $12,000.00. Is that consistent with a 6.2% rate?

choices.text: No; it should be $7,440
No; it should be $174
Yes, because any amount under $1,000 is fine

sources: IRS (Topic 751): Employee Social Security tax is 6.2% (up to the annual wage base) and Medicare tax is 1.45% of wages. (https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751)

questions.prompt: Gabriel's final pay stub shows year-to-date federal tax withheld of $2,140, but Box 2 of his W-2 shows $2,410. What should he do?

choices.text: Ask payroll which amount is correct
Use whichever number gives a bigger refund
Ignore it; the two forms never match
Add the two amounts together on his return

questions.correct_answer: Ask payroll which amount is correct
questions.intro: Each January, employers send Form W-2, which reports the year's wages and taxes withheld. Its totals should match your last pay stub of the year (for wages subject to each tax).
questions.feedback: The totals should match; a difference may be a typo, so ask payroll for a corrected W-2 if needed.

misconceptions.B: Picks a number instead of fixing an error

sources: IRS (Topic 751): Employee Social Security tax is 6.2% (up to the annual wage base) and Medicare tax is 1.45% of wages. (https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751)

questions.prompt: Why keep pay stubs until you have checked your W-2?

choices.text: Because banks require them to deposit paychecks
Because they can be exchanged for cash
Because the IRS requires mailing them in each year
To confirm the W-2's wages and withholding are correct

questions.correct_answer: To confirm the W-2's wages and withholding are correct
questions.feedback: Pay stubs let you verify the W-2 before filing and catch errors early.
